headline: BoringVault (weETHs) bytecode verified on Etherscan, public source repo exists, and multiple recognized-firm audits (0xMacro + Spearbit) cover the Arctic architecture

findings.text: BoringVault at 0x917ceE801a67f933F2e6b33fC0cD1ED2d5909D88 is verified on Etherscan (abiSource: 'etherscan', verified: true). The DeFiPunkd ABI API confirms proxy: null, meaning it is a direct implementation contract — no separate implementation verification check is required.

Public source repo exists at https://github.com/Se7en-Seas/boring-vault and contains BoringVault source code. The ABI sourced from Etherscan is consistent with the BoringVault contract structure described in the repo. A specific commit SHA was not pinned in this run (GitHub fetch was blocked); recorded in unknowns[].

The boring-vault audit folder contains three audit PDFs: 0xmacro-boring-vault-arctic-0.pdf, 0xmacro-boring-vault-arctic-1.pdf, and spearbit-boring-vault-arctic-0.pdf — all targeting the Arctic BoringVault architecture. The 0xMacro sevenSeas-1 audit (March 10, 2024) covered the older cellar-contracts repo at commit 0a7d659064c9070bd369d5c511ba94c6b01bbab2, which is a different (pre-BoringVault) codebase. Veda docs confirm that audit firms Spearbit, Macro, Secure3, and Hexens have all evaluated the BoringVault. A Certora partnership was announced on the protocol website as of the analysis date.

0xMacro and Spearbit are broadly recognized Solidity audit firms. Secure3 and Hexens are not on the canonical recognized-firm list, but they are additive — the primary audits from Spearbit and 0xMacro on the boring-vault Arctic architecture satisfy the recognized-firm requirement. Certora (formal verification) is also on the canonical list per the website announcement.
Post-audit drift could not be assessed: GitHub was inaccessible for a commit-level diff in this run. Drift assessment recorded in unknowns[].
The contract is not a proxy (proxy: null per DeFiPunkd ABI API). No separate implementation contract needs to be verified.

steelman.red: If the boring-vault Arctic audit PDFs cover only peripheral decoder contracts and not the core BoringVault.sol itself, the core vault holding user funds would be effectively un-audited from a recognized firm.
steelman.orange: The sevenSeas-1 0xMacro audit explicitly scoped the older cellar-contracts architecture, not BoringVault; if the Arctic-architecture audit PDFs (in the repo folder but not fully fetched in this run) similarly have limited scope relative to the deployed BoringVault, audit coverage would be incomplete, and no commit SHA was pinned for V2 source correspondence.
steelman.green: The vault bytecode is verified directly on Etherscan (not proxied), the boring-vault GitHub repo is public and corresponds to the deployed contract name and ABI shape, and three audit PDFs from recognized firms (0xMacro twice, Spearbit once) specifically targeting the Arctic BoringVault architecture are stored in the repo's audit folder — meeting all green-grade conditions even without a local bytecode compile-match.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because: (1) V1 is fully satisfied — bytecode verified on Etherscan, not a proxy, no implementation gap; (2) V2 is substantially satisfied — public repo at Se7en-Seas/boring-vault exists and the ABI structure matches the BoringVault contract described in that repo, with the only gap being a pinned commit SHA; (3) V3/V4 are satisfied — Spearbit and 0xMacro (both recognized) audited the boring-vault Arctic architecture with PDFs stored in the repo, and the docs page confirms multiple firms. The orange steelman (stale sevenSeas-1 scope + no commit pin) is weaker than green because the boring-vault-specific audit PDFs are distinct from and post-date the cellar-contracts audit, and the ABI source being 'etherscan' confirms the deployed source is publicly visible.

protocol_metadata.about: Veda (formerly Seven Seas) is a vault infrastructure platform that enables institutions to launch and manage onchain yield products. Users deposit assets into BoringVault contracts, receiving liquid share tokens (e.g. weETHs) in return; a Merkle-tree-based Manager contract constrains which external protocols and calldata the vault can interact with. The platform powers enterprise Earn solutions across 12+ chains, with curators configuring strategies over the pooled assets.
